lesson.title: One-Sided Limits: Approaching From Only One Direction
lesson.summary: A one-sided limit restricts the approach to a single side of the target, left or right, which is exactly the tool needed for functions that behave differently on the two sides of a point.
lesson.body:
So far, "x approaches a" has meant x is allowed to close in on a from either side, left or right, with both directions required to agree. A one-sided limit relaxes that requirement on purpose: it only asks what the function does as x approaches a while staying on one particular side, and it uses a small mark on a to say which side. The notation lim(x to a-) f(x) restricts x to values less than a (approaching from the left), while lim(x to a+) f(x) restricts x to values greater than a (approaching from the right).

One-sided limits matter because plenty of functions genuinely behave differently on the two sides of a point, and a single two-sided limit notation cannot capture that difference; you need the ability to talk about each side separately first. This especially comes up at breakpoints in piecewise-defined functions, at domain boundaries, and at jumps or holes in a graph.

A clean example is the sign function, f(x) = |x|/x, defined for every x not equal to 0. For any x > 0, |x| = x, so f(x) = x/x = 1. For any x < 0, |x| = -x, so f(x) = -x/x = -1. Now examine the one-sided limits as x approaches 0. Approaching from the right, x stays positive the entire time, so f(x) = 1 for every single input tested, and the outputs trivially converge to 1: lim(x to 0+) f(x) = 1. Approaching from the left, x stays negative the entire time, so f(x) = -1 throughout, giving lim(x to 0-) f(x) = -1.

One-sided limits are also unavoidable whenever a function's domain itself only extends in one direction from a point. Take f(x) = sqrt(x), whose domain is restricted to x >= 0 because negative numbers have no real square root. Asking for lim(x to 0-) sqrt(x) does not even make sense, since there are no domain values immediately to the left of 0 to test. But lim(x to 0+) sqrt(x) is perfectly meaningful: as x shrinks toward 0 through positive values, sqrt(x) shrinks toward 0 as well, so lim(x to 0+) sqrt(x) = 0. Here the one-sided limit is not a choice made for convenience, it is the only kind of limit the function's domain allows at this particular point.

Notice these two one-sided limits produced different numbers, 1 and -1, for the very same target a = 0. That is completely allowed: one-sided limits are computed independently of each other, each using only the input values on its designated side, and there is no requirement that they match. The plain, unrestricted limit lim(x to 0) f(x) is a separate question entirely, one that depends on comparing these two one-sided results to each other, which is exactly the comparison the left-hand and right-hand limit ideas coming up next are built to formalize.

Practically, computing a one-sided limit uses the same tools as any other limit: substitution, algebraic simplification, or tables of values, just restricted to inputs approaching from the specified side. The new skill here is not a new calculation technique, but the discipline of tracking which side you are on and reporting only what happens on that side.
